lead: A Maxwell relation is an equality between two partial derivatives of a thermodynamic potential. It exists because U, H, A and G are state functions, so their mixed second derivatives are equal. The equalities replace an entropy derivative, which is hard to measure, with a pressure, volume or temperature derivative, which comes from PVT data. Engineers use them to find entropy changes, enthalpy changes and the Joule–Thomson coefficient. Some syllabi call these Maxwell's thermodynamic relations.
prereq: You need exact differentials from Chapter 4.2, ideal-gas entropy from Unit 3, and free energies from Chapter 4.1.

sections.h3: Where the four relations come from

blocks.text: For a state function F of two variables x and y, dF = M dx + N dy is exact. Exactness means (∂M/∂y)x = (∂N/∂x)y. Apply this test to each fundamental differential from Chapter 4.2.

Symbols: U internal energy (J), H enthalpy (J), A Helmholtz energy (J), G Gibbs energy (J), T absolute temperature (K), S entropy (J/K), P pressure (Pa), V volume (m³). The definitions are H = U + PV, A = U − TS, G = H − TS.

items: dU = T dS − P dV gives (∂T/∂V)<sub>S</sub> = −(∂P/∂S)<sub>V</sub>.
dH = T dS + V dP gives (∂T/∂P)<sub>S</sub> = (∂V/∂S)<sub>P</sub>.

blocks.text: Each line is one Maxwell relation. In the dA and dG relations entropy appears in the numerator of the left side, so those two convert an entropy slope into a P–V–T slope. In the dU and dH relations entropy stays in the derivative, so they are less useful for that job.

The dG relation is the workhorse for entropy changes with pressure at fixed temperature. For an ideal gas, V = nRT/P, so (∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = nR/P. Here n is amount (mol) and R is the gas constant, 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

blocks.where: S is entropy (J/K), P pressure (Pa), V volume (m³), T temperature (K); the subscript T means temperature is held constant.

blocks.text: At constant T, integrate from P1 to P2. For an ideal gas, ΔS = −nR ln(P2/P1). Compression (P2 > P1) lowers entropy because the gas has less volume to occupy.

blocks.where: H is enthalpy (J); the other symbols are as above. Substitute the dG Maxwell relation into dH = T dS + V dP at constant T.

blocks.text: The Joule–Thomson coefficient μ<sub>JT</sub> = (∂T/∂P)<sub>H</sub> follows from the same enthalpy slope. Since dH = Cp dT + (∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub> dP at constant H, μ<sub>JT</sub> = [T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> − V]/Cp. Cp is heat capacity at constant pressure (J/K). An ideal gas has V = nRT/P, so T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = V and μ<sub>JT</sub> = 0.

The variable held constant is part of the derivative. (∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> fixes pressure, not entropy or volume. Dropping the subscript changes the value of the derivative, so always state the variable held constant.

The dA relation can be more convenient when volume data are available: at constant T, ΔS = ∫(∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> dV. For an ideal gas, P = nRT/V, so (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> = nR/V and ΔS = nR ln(V2/V1). This is the same entropy change written with volume ratio.
For a real gas, do not replace (∂V/∂T)P by nR/P. Use measured or equation-of-state values of V and its temperature slope. Residual-property formulas built from these derivatives are in Chapter 4.4.

spec.title: Four differentials give four Maxwell relations
spec.aria: The four exact differentials dU, dH, dA and dG are connected by Legendre transforms; each gives one Maxwell relation by equal mixed second derivatives.

examples.question: Use a Maxwell relation to calculate ΔS when 2 mol of ideal gas at 300 K is compressed from 1 bar to 10 bar at constant temperature.
steps: Start from dG = −S dT + V dP. Exactness gives (∂S/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = −(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub>.
For an ideal gas PV = nRT, so V = nRT/P. At constant P, (∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = nR/P.
Integrate at constant T from P1 = 1 bar to P2 = 10 bar: ΔS = −nR ln(P2/P1).
Apply the negative sign: ΔS = −38.29 J/K, which rounds to −38.3 J/K. The 300 K value does not enter the ideal-gas pressure formula.
examples.check:
import math
n = 2.0
R = 8.314
P1 = 1.0
P2 = 10.0
dS = -n * R * math.log(P2 / P1)
print(round(dS, 1))

traps: Sign slip: (∂S/∂P)<sub>T</sub> is negative for an ideal gas; compression at constant T lowers entropy.
Wrong constant variable: (∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> is not the same as (∂V/∂T)<sub>S</sub> or (∂V/∂P)<sub>T</sub>.
Celsius instead of kelvin: T in (∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub> and μ<sub>JT</sub> must be absolute temperature.
Using nR/P for a real gas: that slope is only the ideal-gas value.
Mixing dA and dG signs: dA has −S dT − P dV, while dG has −S dT + V dP.

quiz.q: Write the Maxwell relation obtained from dG = −S dT + V dP.
Why are Maxwell relations useful in property calculations?
quiz.a: They replace an entropy derivative, which is hard to measure, by a P, V, T derivative that comes from PVT data or an equation of state.

quiz.q: One mole of ideal gas at 300 K is compressed from 1 bar to 5 bar at constant T. Find ΔS using a Maxwell relation.

quiz.a: For an ideal gas (∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> = V/T, so (∂H/∂P)<sub>T</sub> = V − T(V/T) = 0.

quiz.q: A real gas has T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> < V. Find μ<sub>JT</sub> and state whether expansion through a throttle warms or cools the gas.
quiz.a: μ<sub>JT</sub> = [T(∂V/∂T)<sub>P</sub> − V]/Cp; the numerator is negative, so μ<sub>JT</sub> < 0. For expansion dP < 0, and dT = μ<sub>JT</sub> dP > 0, so the gas warms.

quiz.q: Explain why ΔS = ∫(∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub> dV at constant T is valid for any simple compressible substance.
quiz.a: It follows from the exact differential dA = −S dT − P dV and the Maxwell relation (∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub> = (∂P/∂T)<sub>V</sub>. At constant T, dS = (∂S/∂V)<sub>T</sub> dV, then integrate.

beyond: Not for the exam. Maxwell relations are used as thermodynamic consistency checks for equations of state and for deriving fugacity-coefficient slopes in Unit 5. Process simulators rely on them to convert one measured derivative into another. Search next for Maxwell relations with residual properties and the Joule–Thomson coefficient of real gases.
